Good morning everyone and welcome to the Riverside Science Museum. My name is Oliver and I'll be giving you a quick introduction before you explore on your own. Before describing the individual features of this Science Museum tour, it is useful to understand the overall sequence. The information for the Science Museum tour follows the order in which most people encounter the site or activity, following the main route before considering possible variations. Knowing that sequence will make the later directions and choices in the Science Museum tour easier to follow. Let me start with what's changed since your last visit. This year we've opened two brand new attractions that I'd encourage you all to see. The first is a planetarium on the top floor where you can lie back and watch the night sky. The second is our outdoor energy garden where science comes to life in the open air. We've also refurbished the cafe and updated the gift shop. And of course the ever popular flight gallery is still here, exactly where it always was. Some arrangements connected with the Science Museum tour may depend on the time of day or the number of visitors. During the Science Museum tour, listen for the difference between a permanent feature and something available only at a stated time. Where a condition in the Science Museum tour is fixed, it will be presented as a rule. Where there is flexibility, it will be described as a recommendation. Now for some practical information. Guided tours of the main galleries leave every 40 minutes from the information desk in the entrance hall. Each guided tour lasts about an hour, so do allow enough time. If you're carrying bags, please leave them in the cloakroom on the ground floor as large rucksacks aren't permitted in the galleries. Lockers are also available and they cost £2. As the Science Museum tour continues, staff may direct different groups along slightly different routes. Within the Science Museum tour, a change to a minor detail does not necessarily alter the main program. If an alternative becomes necessary during the Science Museum tour, wait for the full announcement before moving, because the first place mentioned may be the one that is no longer available. Photography is welcome throughout the building, but we do ask you to switch off your flash, because it can damage some of the more delicate exhibits. Now review, questions 16-20 before the recording continues. Do not try to memorize every detail of the Science Museum tour at once. The key locations and decisions will be repeated in context. For now, concentrate on where the activity begins, which direction or sequence applies, and the point at which you may need to make a choice or ask a member of staff. A final way to follow the Science Museum tour is to separate descriptive information from an instruction that requires action. General advice supports the visit, while a firm instruction must be followed. Keeping those functions separate will prevent an interesting detail from being mistaken for a change to the program. Let me point out a few highlights. On the ground floor, our star attraction is a giant model heart, which is so big that you can actually walk right through it. Upstairs, in the space gallery, you'll be able to see a genuine piece of moon rock brought back by astronauts. And outside in the energy garden, you can try generating electricity yourself by peddling a bicycle. If you become uncertain during the Science Museum tour, pause at the next staffed point rather than following another group without checking. Explain the last location or instruction you clearly remember, and staff can reconnect you with the correct sequence. This is especially important when two activities begin near one another, or when a temporary diversion changes only one section of the route. The program is designed to allow questions, so asking for clarification will not make you miss the main activity. Finally, don't leave without visiting our temporary exhibition, which this season is all about robots. It runs until the end of August. Members receive a 20% discount in the shop, and children under 5 come in free. Enjoy your visit and please ask any of our staff if you need help. Before the Science Museum tour moves to its final practical details, remember that similar locations or services may have different conditions. Listen for the full name, the direction attached to it, and any time restriction. A descriptive example may help you recognise a place, but only a direct instruction tells you to change route, or take action. If a temporary arrangement replaces the normal one, the replacement will be stated after the original is identified. This final distinction connects the earlier overview with the choices that follow and helps prevent a familiar name from being confused with the service currently available. Part 2 is complete. In today's lecture, I want to look at one of the greatest challenges in the shift to clean power, how we store energy from renewable sources. To place the energy storage lecture in perspective, we need to distinguish the familiar modern description from the longer process that produced it. Within the energy storage lecture, what now appears stable often emerged through several pathways rather than one smooth sequence. A simple list of events in the energy storage lecture can hide those alternatives, so the discussion will emphasize why particular changes mattered. The problem starts with the nature of renewables themselves. Sources such as solar panels and wind farms are intermittent, which means they only generate electricity when the sun is shining or the wind is blowing, and not at other times. Because supply and use rarely match, we need to capture surplus power and release it later, during periods of high demand. For instance, on a cold winter evening when everyone switches on the heating. Evidence for the energy storage lecture does not come from a single source. Researchers may compare historical material with evidence gathered using modern instruments. Each source answers a different question and carries its own uncertainty. Agreement can increase confidence while disagreement often reveals an assumption or a measurement problem that deserves closer examination. So, what are the options? The most widespread storage technology today relies on lithium-ion batteries like those found in phones and electric cars, only on a much larger scale. A much older method is pumped hydro. When there is spare electricity, it is used to pump water uphill into a reservoir. Later, when power is needed, that water is released and flows back down through a turbine, which spins to generate electricity all over again. Scale is especially important when evaluating the energy storage lecture. A process observed in one case, one community or one short trial may behave differently across a region or over several generations. In this energy storage lecture, the lecture will return to this distinction in each case study. This comparison helps identify which conditions are essential and which are merely helpful. There are other clever approaches too. In compressed air storage, surplus electricity squeezes air into sealed underground caves. When demand rises, the air is let out to drive a generator. And in some solar power plants, mirrors focus the sun's heat to melt salt. The molten salt stays hot for many hours and can later boil water into steam. It is also worth noticing the language of certainty used in the energy storage lecture. Some mechanisms are supported by direct observation, while others remain the best explanation available from indirect evidence. Scientific caution does not mean that every account is equally likely. Keep that distinction in mind as the examples are brought together. The separate examples in the energy storage lecture can finally be organized around three questions. What conditions begin a change, which mechanisms sustain it, and what consequences appear later. For the energy storage lecture, it also makes similarities visible without pretending that every case is identical. The conclusion to the energy storage lecture will use that framework to connect the details without extending them beyond the available evidence. Of course, every method has its drawbacks. Batteries, although efficient, remain expensive, and their lifespan is limited because after a certain number of charges they must be replaced. Worse still, the metals inside them, such as lithium and cobalt, are difficult and sometimes environmentally damaging to mine. A useful final check is to ask what observation would make the present account of the energy storage lecture less convincing. Identifying such evidence keeps the explanation testable and reveals where future research would be most informative. It also prevents a plausible narrative from being treated as complete merely because its separate examples fit together. Looking to the future, researchers are pursuing fresh ideas. One is to store spare renewable electricity in the form of hydrogen gas, which can be burned or fed into fuel cells whenever it is needed. Others are designing cheaper batteries that avoid rare metals altogether. With better storage, renewable energy could one day power our homes and cities around the clock. One final point about the energy storage lecture concerns the difference between a useful model and a complete explanation. A model selects the relationships that matter most for a particular question, so it can be informative even when it leaves out local variation. Problems arise when that simplification is forgotten and a result from one scale is treated as a rule for every case. The evidence discussed here should therefore be read with its conditions attached. The period observed, the population or material studied, the method used and the uncertainty that remains. Those conditions do not weaken the account. They show exactly where the conclusion is supported and where further observation would be needed.
